name: Backpropagation
statement: Train a neural network by sending the error backward through it to find each weight's gradient.
statementAccent: sending the error backward through it to find each weight's gradient
meaning: Backpropagation, short for backward propagation of errors, is the fundamental algorithm used to train artificial neural networks. It efficiently computes the gradient of a loss, or error, function with respect to the network's weights, so that the weights can then be adjusted, typically by gradient descent, to reduce the error. Backpropagation is an application of the chain rule of calculus to the network. Training proceeds in two phases. In the forward pass, an input is fed through the network layer by layer to produce an output, and the intermediate activations are cached; the output is compared to the desired target to compute the loss. In the backward pass, the error is propagated backward through the network, one layer at a time from the output layer to the input layer, computing how much each weight contributed to the error, which is exactly the gradient of the loss with respect to that weight. Because it reuses the cached intermediate values rather than recomputing them, backpropagation finds all the gradients efficiently, at a cost comparable to a forward pass, instead of the far more expensive approach of perturbing each weight separately. The algorithm was brought to prominence by a famous 1986 paper in Nature by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams, though its underlying ideas have earlier roots, in Paul Werbos's 1974 doctoral thesis and Seppo Linnainmaa's 1970 description of reverse-mode automatic differentiation. Backpropagation is the workhorse that makes modern deep learning possible.
mechanism: Backpropagation computes the gradient of a neural network's loss function with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule of calculus systematically and efficiently. A neural network is a composition of many simple functions, layers of weighted sums passed through nonlinear activation functions, and the loss is a function of the final output. To adjust the weights to reduce the loss, one needs the partial derivative of the loss with respect to each weight, and computing these naively, by perturbing each weight and re-running the network, would be hopelessly slow for networks with millions of parameters. Backpropagation avoids this. First comes the forward pass: the input propagates through the layers to produce an output, with each layer's activations stored. The loss is then computed by comparing the output to the target. Then comes the backward pass: starting at the output, the algorithm computes the derivative of the loss with respect to the output, and then propagates these derivatives backward, one layer at a time, using the chain rule to express the derivative at each layer in terms of the derivative at the next layer and the layer's own weights and activations. This reuse of already-computed quantities, in a manner reminiscent of dynamic programming, is what makes it efficient: all the gradients are obtained in a single backward sweep whose cost is comparable to the forward pass. The resulting gradients are handed to an optimizer, usually a variant of gradient descent, which nudges each weight in the direction that reduces the loss. Repeated over many examples, this is how networks learn. Backpropagation requires the activation functions to be differentiable, and in very deep networks the repeated multiplication of derivatives can cause vanishing or exploding gradients.

examples.text: The forward pass produces an output and caches activations; the backward pass propagates the error to get gradients.
Backpropagation is the chain rule applied layer by layer, expressing each layer's gradient via the next.
All gradients are found in one backward sweep at roughly the cost of a forward pass, not by perturbing each weight.

whyItMatters: Backpropagation is the algorithm that makes modern deep learning possible, the engine that trains essentially every deep neural network in use today, from image classifiers and speech recognizers to the large language models behind contemporary artificial intelligence. Training a network means adjusting its weights to reduce error, and doing so requires knowing how the error changes with each of possibly billions of weights; backpropagation computes all of these gradients efficiently, in a single backward pass, turning what would otherwise be an impossibly expensive computation into a routine one. Without it, training large networks would be infeasible, and the deep-learning revolution of the last decade could not have happened. Its intellectual significance is equally large: backpropagation is a beautiful, general application of the chain rule, and the same idea, reverse-mode automatic differentiation, underlies the software frameworks that power the field. The famous 1986 paper by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams showed that backpropagation could discover useful internal representations in a network's hidden layers, a result that helped revive interest in neural networks, while the layered history reaching back to Linnainmaa and Werbos is a reminder of how ideas mature. As the method that trains neural networks by sending error backward to find each weight's gradient, backpropagation is foundational to artificial intelligence.

propagate the error backward layer by layer via the chain rule to get each weight's gradient.
hand the gradients to an optimizer, usually gradient descent, to adjust the weights and reduce the loss.

limits: Backpropagation is the standard training method, but several points reward care. It requires the network's activation functions to be differentiable, since it relies on derivatives; non-differentiable components need special handling. It computes a gradient, which drives the loss toward a local minimum, not necessarily the global one, and on the non-convex loss surfaces of deep networks the optimizer may settle in a local minimum or slow near a saddle point. In very deep networks the repeated multiplication of small or large derivatives through many layers can cause vanishing or exploding gradients, a real practical obstacle addressed by architectural and normalization techniques. The history rewards care: the algorithm was popularized, not invented, by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams in 1986; the essential method of reverse-mode automatic differentiation was described by Seppo Linnainmaa in 1970 and applied to neural networks by Paul Werbos, so crediting the 1986 paper with the invention overlooks that lineage. Backpropagation computes gradients; it is the accompanying optimizer, not backpropagation itself, that updates the weights. So backpropagation robustly computes neural-network gradients, understood as an efficient application of the chain rule with a layered history and real optimization limits.
misreadings: Backpropagation is not the whole of learning but the computation of gradients; a separate optimizer, usually gradient descent, actually updates the weights. It does not guarantee the global minimum, only a local one on non-convex surfaces. And it was popularized, not invented, in 1986, with roots in Linnainmaa 1970 and Werbos 1974, so treating backprop as the optimizer itself, as finding the global optimum, or as originating wholly in 1986, misreads it.
origin: The algorithm for training neural networks, an efficient chain-rule computation of loss gradients popularized by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams in 1986 with roots in Linnainmaa (1970) and Werbos (1974).
